Apps assigned the correct urgency level in 49 percent of vignettes on average, ranging from 33 to 71 percent between apps. Emergency vignettes were correctly advised to seek emergency care in 78 percent of cases. Over-triage was common: 41 percent of self-care vignettes were advised to see a doctor or attend an emergency department. Results varied more between apps than between vignette types. Vignettes were entered by researchers, not by patients."},{"title":"Symptom checker advice compared with nurse telephone triage for the same callers: a prospective comparison","authors":"Okafor-Lindgren T, Beaulieu-Asante R","year":2024,"venue":"Emergency Access Research","doi":"10.5555/ear.2024.0137","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Callers to a regional telephone advice line were invited to use a symptom checker app before speaking to a triage nurse; 1,210 callers completed both. App and nurse urgency levels agreed for 61 percent of callers. The app advised a lower urgency than the nurse for 11 percent of callers, including 3 of the 46 callers whom the nurse sent to an emergency department. Agreement was lower for callers aged over 70 (52 percent). The nurse was not blinded to the app's advice in the first month of the study."},{"title":"Do symptom checkers work for children? A vignette study of paediatric presentations","authors":"Marsden-Achieng P, Ruiz-Takahashi L","year":2021,"venue":"Paediatric Digital Health","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We tested eight symptom checker apps with 90 paediatric vignettes written by paediatric emergency physicians. Apps correctly identified the need for emergency care in 64 percent of emergency vignettes and assigned the correct urgency level overall in 42 percent. Three of the eight apps were not designed for children but gave advice when a child's age was entered. Fever in infants under three months was under-triaged by five apps. Parents did not enter the vignettes, so real-world accuracy may differ."},{"title":"Vignette-based evaluation of digital triage tools: a methodological critique","authors":"Hughes-Ndiaye C, Moreau-Kristiansen A, Tan-Oyelaran F","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Digital Triage","doi":"10.5555/jdt.2019.0012","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Most evaluations of symptom checkers enter vignettes written by clinicians in textbook language. We rewrote 60 vignettes in the words lay users chose when describing the same scenarios, and entered both versions into five apps. Accuracy for the correct urgency level was 12 percentage points lower with lay-worded vignettes. Differences were largest for chest pain and abdominal pain scenarios, where lay users described location and timing less precisely. We argue that clinician-written vignettes overstate real-world accuracy and that studies with real users are needed before endorsement."},{"title":"App version changes and the stability of triage accuracy over 18 months","authors":"Ferreira-Blackwood N, Adeyemi-Strand O","year":2025,"venue":"Digital Health Evaluation","doi":"10.5555/dhe.2025.0048","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We re-tested three symptom checker apps with the same 120 vignettes every six months for 18 months. Over this period each app released between four and seven updates. Accuracy for the correct urgency level varied by up to 14 percentage points between versions of the same app. One app's advice for emergency vignettes improved from 70 to 85 percent correct, while another's declined from 81 to 69 percent. Developers did not publish what had changed. We recommend that any endorsement be tied to a version and re-tested."},{"title":"Language, health literacy and symptom checker use: an observational study in an urgent care waiting room","authors":"Nwosu-Harrington E, Castellanos-Pike D","year":2020,"venue":"Emergency Access Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We invited 312 patients waiting in an urgent care centre to use a symptom checker app before being seen. Patients with limited English or low health literacy abandoned the app before receiving advice more often than other patients (29 against 9 percent). When they completed it, they more often received advice of lower urgency than the clinician's assessment. Translated versions of the app were available but rarely chosen, often because the language setting was hard to find. The study was conducted in one centre over three months."}]}
